title: Tool admission table — a declarative single source of truth for which tools reach the model
one_line: Replace the 25-branch `if (name === …)` ladder inside `isToolAllowed` with one `Map` of tool-name → admission rule, so a built-in tool's admission is a single data entry instead of a position in a chain, and make the four parallel tool-name declarations provably agree.
user_visible_effect: none directly — the exact same set of tools reaches the model before and after. It becomes visible only through the refactors it unblocks: moving a built-in tool out to an extension becomes a one-file mechanical edit instead of a four-file change, and a new built-in can no longer be added without an admission decision, because the table is compile-time exhaustive.
effort: M (~1.5 days). Mostly careful mechanical work plus a characterization test that must be written and proven green BEFORE the refactor, not after.
risk: The `isToolAllowed` closure captures eleven values (`session`, `restrictToolNames`, `requestedTools`, `includeYield`, `enableLsp`, `goalEnabled`, `externalThinkingActive`, `allowEval`, and every `cfg*.get(session.settings)` read). Hoisting each branch into a standalone `(ctx) => boolean` forces every one of those to become an explicit context field; a dropped field compiles cleanly and silently widens or narrows admission. The one that bites hardest is `requestedTools`, which is not a snapshot — it is a live array that `isToolAllowed` reads at call time *after* `requestedTools.push("yield")` has already mutated it at `tools/index.ts:794-796`.

steps.instruction: BEFORE touching anything, write the characterization test (step 2) and get it green against the CURRENT if-chain. The plan's own warning is right that this is where the work goes wrong; the only defence is a test that was red when the behaviour differed, and that test is worthless if written after the refactor.

Build a `makeSession(overrides)` helper modelled on the one at `packages/coding-agent/test/issue-5764-registertool-loadmode.test.ts:22-29` — it MUST set `skipPythonPreflight: true` or `resolveBuiltinToolPlan` awaits a real Python kernel probe. Drive every row through the exported `resolveBuiltinToolPlan(session, toolNames)` and assert on the resolved `.names` list, never on table internals (AGENTS.md: assert the observable contract, and the plan agrees the contract is 'which tools the model is given').

Add exactly six table rows, each a DISTINCT branch, no duplicates: (a) `goal` three-way — goal.enabled off, and the `getGoalModeState()` states `undefined` / `{enabled:false}` / `{enabled:false, status:"dropped"}`; (b) `wait` three-way OR — each of async / irc / launch alone, plus all three off, since the OR is the whole rule; (c) `checkpoint`+`rewind` depth-gated pair at `taskDepth` 0 and 1, with and without an explicit tool list; (d) `manage_skill` autolearn on/off crossed with the same depth matrix; (e) `learn` = (d) plus the memory-backend axis (`local` admitted, a non-listed backend not); (f) `task` via `canSpawnAtDepth` at the recursion limit — this is a genuinely different fork (it reads `cfgTaskMaxRecursionDepth`, not the `taskDepth === 0` term), which is why it earns a row instead of being folded into (c)/(d).

Add the row the plan calls mandatory and the one that fails first: an extension-registered tool name that is NOT a built-in must survive `resolveBuiltinToolPlan` unchanged under EVERY settings combination. Iterate a representative settings matrix (all gates off, all gates on, memory backend `mnemopi`, autolearn on, goal mode on) and assert the extension name is in `.names` each time.

Add the prototype-safety row: an extension tool named `toString` (and `constructor`) must be admitted, and one named `__proto__` must be admitted without throwing. This is a NEW contract the old code satisfies by accident (the if-chain fell through to `return true`) and a naive `Record` lookup would break. Pin it before the refactor so the failure is observable.

Commit the characterization test on its own, with the production code untouched. Confirm it is green. If it is not, the if-chain is not what the plan says it is — stop and re-read `tools/index.ts:731-793`.

Create the new module. Declare the `ToolAdmissionContext` interface with ONE field per closure capture listed in `risk`, then the `ADMISSION_RULES` object annotated `satisfies Record<BuiltinToolName | HiddenToolName, ToolAdmissionRule>` — the union, NOT `ToolName`, because `goal` and `think` are `HiddenToolName` and `ToolName = BuiltinToolName` (`tools/index.ts:593`). Give `read`/`write`/`edit`/`yield` explicit `() => true` entries: they had no branch in the old chain, and stating them makes the table a complete description of admission instead of a partial one.

Export `TOOL_ADMISSION: ReadonlyMap<string, ToolAdmissionRule> = new Map(Object.entries(ADMISSION_RULES))` and the `isToolAllowed(name, ctx)` helper whose lookup is `TOOL_ADMISSION.get(name)?.(ctx) ?? true`. The `Map` wrapper is deliberate and load-bearing — do not simplify it back to a bare object; the reason is in `code_shape` and is reproduced in plan_corrections.

Delete the 25-branch ladder wholesale and replace it with a single `admissionCtx` object literal plus `const isToolAllowed = (name: string) => evaluateToolAdmission(name, admissionCtx)`. Keep the exported shape of `BuiltinToolPlan.isAllowed` (`tools/index.ts:611`) byte-identical — `sdk.ts:3350` calls it in the live settings reconcile and must not need a change.

Audit the ORDER of the `requestedTools` mutations relative to the `admissionCtx` construction. `requestedTools.push("yield")` at `:794-796` runs AFTER `isToolAllowed` is defined but BEFORE it is called at `:799`/`:801`; the three depth-gated rules read `ctx.requestedTools !== undefined`, a reference check that survives the push, so behaviour is preserved — but verify it rather than assuming, and do NOT snapshot `requestedTools` into the context as a copy.

Optional but strongly recommended, and the natural moment for it: `defaultLoadModeForToolName` uses `name in ESSENTIAL_BUILTIN_TOOL_NAMES` on an object literal, so `defaultLoadModeForToolName("toString")` returns `"essential"` today — Object.prototype keys satisfy `in`. Switch to `Object.hasOwn(ESSENTIAL_BUILTIN_TOOL_NAMES, name)`. This is a pre-existing bug, not a regression you introduce; note it as such in the PR so it is not confused with the table work.

Address the 'one source of truth' half. `BUILTIN_TOOL_NAMES` ↔ `BUILTIN_TOOLS` is ALREADY compile-time enforced (`tools/index.ts:554`, `Record<BuiltinToolName, ToolFactory>` — tsc errors on both a missing and an extra key), so there is nothing to merge there. The two declarations with NO type link are `ESSENTIAL_BUILTIN_TOOL_NAMES` (`Record<string, true>`, untyped keys, guarded only by the runtime test at `issue-5764-registertool-loadmode.test.ts:113`) and `SESSION_MANAGED_BUILTIN_TOOL_NAMES` (`sdk.ts:1161`, a bare string array). Give the latter the `readonly BuiltinToolName[]` annotation, which is a one-line change that converts a silent drift into a compile error. Leave `ESSENTIAL_BUILTIN_TOOL_NAMES` as a runtime-verified record — it is keyed by tool class behaviour, not by name identity, and the existing guard is the right instrument for it.

gate: The characterization test from steps 2-6, written and committed BEFORE the refactor, green both before and after. Concretely, all six branch rows plus the extension-tool row plus the prototype-safety row must pass against BOTH the 25-branch chain and the table. Add a manual one-time audit: diff the resolved `.names` for all 33 tool names across a settings×depth matrix (taskDepth 0 and 1 × gates-all-off and gates-all-on × memory backend `hindsight`/`mnemopi`/`local`) between the pre-refactor commit and the post-refactor commit — the two must be byte-identical. This is the check the plan asks for and it is the one that catches a dropped closure capture, which no assertion in the test file can catch by itself.
test_contract: Defends: 'the set of tools a session is given does not change when the admission ladder becomes a table'. A consumer regression here is silent and severe — an extra tool in the schema costs tokens and confuses the model, a missing tool makes a capability unreachable with no error anywhere. Specifically it pins: the three-way `goal` rule including the `dropped`-status exception; the three-way OR in `wait`; the three depth-gated rules sharing the `taskDepth === 0 || requestedTools !== undefined` term; `task`'s separate `canSpawnAtDepth` fork; and default-allow for anything that is not a built-in. The prototype-safety row is the one that catches a naive `Record` implementation, and the extension-tool row is the one that catches a table accidentally keyed on the wrong union or a lookup that misses its `?? true` default.

plan_corrections.claim: The risk is 'silent priority inversion': the 25-branch chain is an early-return ladder, so reordering branches during the move can change which rule wins without changing any rule's body.
plan_corrections.verdict: OVERSTATED — and pointing the implementer at it will waste the day they should spend on the real risk
plan_corrections.correction: All 25 branches are `if (name === "literal")` and the 29 distinct names across them are pairwise disjoint, so at most one branch can ever match a given `name`. Branch order therefore provably cannot change any outcome; the stated failure mode cannot occur. The REAL risk is the one the plan does not name: hoisting each branch into a standalone `(ctx) => boolean` requires promoting eleven closure captures to explicit context fields, and a dropped field compiles cleanly while silently changing admission. The mechanical move is order-insensitive; the semantic move is capture-insensitive.

plan_corrections.correction: `ToolName = BuiltinToolName` (`tools/index.ts:593`), which is the 30 built-in names. But `isToolAllowed` carries real, non-default rules for `goal` and `think`, and both are `HiddenToolName`, not `BuiltinToolName`. The key must be `BuiltinToolName | HiddenToolName` (33 names). Writing it as the plan states either fails the typecheck or silently drops the `goal` rule — and the `goal` rule is the one carrying a three-way condition and a `dropped`-status exception.
plan_corrections.evidence: `grep -n 'export type ToolName' tools/index.ts` → `593: export type ToolName = BuiltinToolName;`. `builtin-names.ts:36` shows `HIDDEN_TOOL_NAMES = ["yield", "goal", "think"]`. The branch list contains `goal` and `think`; subtracting the 30 `BUILTIN_TOOL_NAMES` leaves exactly those two as covered-but-not-builtin.

plan_corrections.claim: Not mentioned anywhere in the plan: a `Record`-shaped admission table introduces a prototype-chain lookup hazard that the current if-chain does not have.
plan_corrections.verdict: NEW FINDING — this is the sharpest correctness risk in the item
plan_corrections.correction: With a plain object literal and a `TABLE[name]` lookup, `TABLE["toString"]` resolves to `Object.prototype.toString` — a FUNCTION, so calling it returns the truthy string `"[object Undefined]"` instead of a boolean; `TABLE["constructor"]` returns `Object`, truthy; `TABLE["__proto__"]` returns a non-function that THROWS when called. The current if-chain is immune because unmatched names fall through to `return true`. This is reachable, not theoretical: `tools/index.ts:799` gates on `name in BUILTIN_TOOLS`, and `in` on an object literal is exactly as prototype-polluted — an extension tool named `toString` already passes that gate today and reaches `isToolAllowed`. Mitigation: build the `Map` from `Object.entries()` of a `satisfies Record<…>` literal, which keeps compile-time exhaustiveness while making lookup prototype-safe.
plan_corrections.evidence: Executed a probe against the real gate shape: `["read","toString","constructor","__proto__"].filter(n => n in BUILTIN_TOOLS)` → all four pass. And against the proposed table: `toString`/`constructor` → callable, truthy non-boolean; `__proto__`/`my_ext_tool` → not callable, throws.

plan_corrections.correction: `BUILTIN_TOOL_NAMES` ↔ `BUILTIN_TOOLS` is ALREADY compile-time enforced: `BUILTIN_TOOLS` is declared `Record<BuiltinToolName, ToolFactory>` (`tools/index.ts:554`), and TypeScript rejects both a missing key and an unknown extra key. There is nothing to merge there and no test to add. The declarations that genuinely lack a type link are `ESSENTIAL_BUILTIN_TOOL_NAMES` (`Record<string, true>` — untyped keys, runtime-only guard) and `SESSION_MANAGED_BUILTIN_TOOL_NAMES` (`sdk.ts:1161`, bare `string[]`, no guard at all). The plan also never mentions the latter.
